Fat transfer is the best-supported option for lasting volume, but it involves liposuction and delivers modest, variable gains. External expansion before grafting may increase them. Do breast enlargement pills work? A medical review found no published clinical trials of bust-enhancing herbal products and discouraged their use. There is no controlled trial showing that any pill enlarges the breasts. Do creams and massage work? No reliable evidence shows that they enlarge breasts. They can improve how the skin feels. Do chest exercises make breasts bigger? They build the muscle beneath the breast and can improve firmness and posture, but they do not increase breast tissue. Is filler a safe shortcut? The FDA recommends against filler for breast enlargement and has not approved any for this use. Risks include nodules, migration, imaging problems and difficulty removing the material. Is fat transfer safe? It is widely used, but one review reported an overall complication rate of 27.8%, with fat necrosis the most common. Discuss the risks with a qualified surgeon. How many cup sizes can I realistically gain without surgery? Bras and padding add about a cup visually. Fat transfer is typically around one cup per session. More usually needs implants. Will it affect mammograms? Fat grafting and fillers can both cause imaging changes. Always tell your radiographer. Why do so many people say supplements worked for them? Temporary swelling, cycle changes, small weight gains and better bras can look like growth, and success stories are shared more than failures. What is the single best first step? A professional bra fitting. It costs little, carries no risk, and often changes the look more than people expect. Non-Surgical Breast Enlargement Non-Surgical Breast Enhancement: Options & Safety Non-surgical treatments differ widely in their intended effects, evidence and regulatory status. This section explains those differences clearly, without advertising claims. Home/Non-Surgical Breast Enlargement/Non-Surgical Breast Enhancement: Options & Safety For the individual evidence guides, explore the Non-Surgical Breast Enlargement section. Treatments marketed as “non-surgical breast enlargement” are not a single category. They include injectable fillers, platelet-rich plasma (PRP), thread-based procedures and collagen-stimulating biostimulators. Each has a different intended effect, a different evidence base and a different regulatory position.Crucially, being non-surgical does not automatically mean a treatment is safe, and not every treatment marketed for this purpose has been demonstrated to reliably increase breast volume. This section is written to help you understand those distinctions before any clinical consultation. The most important pointDermal fillers are not approved for breast enlargement, and the FDA advises against using fillers or other injectable fillers to increase breast size because of potentially serious complications. Regenerative and biostimulatory products require careful scrutiny of their evidence and regulatory status before any claim of benefit is accepted. Assessing any non-surgical claim Six questions worth asking Any advertised non-surgical breast treatment should withstand these questions before you consider it. 01 What is the exact product and intended use?Ask for the precise product name, its approved indications and whether breast use is authorised in your jurisdiction. 02 Is it approved for this purpose?Facial approval does not imply approval for injection into the breasts. Products and permitted uses vary by country. 03 What does the evidence actually show?Distinguish marketing claims from peer-reviewed evidence for the specific procedure being offered. 04 Who is performing it, and with what competence?Suitability depends on the precise product, intended use, clinician competence and applicable regulation. 05 What are the risks and possible complications?Ask about infection, pain, tissue damage, nodules, asymmetry and how complications would be managed. 06 What are the alternatives?Consider evidence-based alternatives for increasing breast volume, including surgical options where relevant. At a glance Primary consideration and key limitation Primary consideration and key limitation OptionPrimary considerationImportant limitation Dermal fillersProduct-specific approved indicationsNot FDA-approved for breast enlargement PRPEvidence for the particular intended useShould not be promoted as proven breast enlargement Threads & mono threadsProduct-specific aesthetic indicationsNot established substitutes for breast augmentation Sculptra / biostimulatorsProduct-specific authorised usesDo not assume suitability for breast-volume enhancement Stem-cell approachesEvidence and regulatory status of the exact productMany marketed regenerative uses remain unapproved or investigational This table covers non-surgical options only. For a side-by-side view including surgical routes (implants and fat transfer), see the full treatment comparison. It should not be read to suggest that a non-surgical procedure is automatically safer than surgery. Questions Non-surgical treatment FAQs What is the safest non-surgical way to make breasts look bigger? A properly fitted bra, padding, clothing choices and posture change the look immediately and carry no medical risk — but they change appearance, not breast tissue. For a method-by-method verdict on every popular approach, read the evidence guide. Does “regenerative” mean a treatment is effective? No. The term describes an area of ongoing research, not proof of effectiveness, approval or suitability for breast enhancement. Products and permitted uses vary by jurisdiction. Where can I find answers about fillers, PRP, fat transfer and surgery? Each treatment page on this website answers its own specific questions, and the most common cross-cutting questions are consolidated on the main FAQs page, with links into the detailed guides. Non-Surgical Breast Enlargement Breast Fillers: Safety, Evidence & Alternatives Dermal fillers are injectable products used for certain approved aesthetic indications. Their use for breast enlargement is a different matter and is not established, approved or routine. Home/Non-Surgical Breast Enlargement/Breast Fillers: Safety, Evidence & Alternatives Regulatory positionThe FDA advises against using dermal fillers or other injectable fillers to increase breast size. Serious complications from inappropriate body injections can include infection, persistent pain, tissue damage, scarring, deformity and potentially life-threatening events. What dermal fillers areDermal fillers are injectable products used for certain approved aesthetic indications, depending on the product and the jurisdiction. Different products have different compositions, behaviours and licensed uses.Why breast use is differentAn approval for facial use does not imply suitability for injection into the breasts. The breast is a different anatomical site with different considerations, and the consequences of complications can be more difficult to manage. Because of this, breast filler injections should not be advertised or presented as a routine breast-enlargement service. What this page should help you understand Safety and decision points Potential complications The difficulty of managing some injected materials, and why complications can be serious or persistent. Evidence-based alternatives Options for people seeking increased breast volume that are supported by clearer evidence. Independent advice The importance of independent medical advice before considering any advertised treatment. Product-specific questionsAsk for the exact product, its approved indications, whether breast use is authorised in your jurisdiction, and how complications would be managed. Further reading from the consolidated articleU.S. FDA — Dermal fillers and their approved usesU.S. FDA — Regenerative medicine and stem cell safety Questions Dermal filler FAQs Are breast fillers approved? Dermal fillers are not approved for breast enlargement. Regulators advise against using them for this purpose because of potentially serious complications. What alternatives exist for added volume? Alternatives with clearer evidence for increasing breast volume include surgical options such as implants or, in selected cases, autologous fat transfer. Suitability depends on individual factors and should be assessed by an appropriately qualified clinician. Non-Surgical Breast Enlargement PRP and Breast Enhancement: Evidence Explained Platelet-rich plasma is prepared from your own blood to concentrate platelets. Its effects depend entirely on the specific indication and the evidence available for it. Home/Non-Surgical Breast Enlargement/PRP and Breast Enhancement: Evidence Explained How PRP is preparedPRP is prepared by taking a sample of the patient’s own blood and processing it to concentrate the platelets. The resulting preparation is intended for specific purposes; those purposes are not interchangeable, and a preparation intended for one indication is not automatically appropriate for another.PRP and breast enhancementClaims about PRP and breast enhancement should be assessed against appropriate clinical evidence for the precise procedure being offered. The evidence for a particular use should be established before that use is described as effective.Conceptual educational illustration; not a patient, treatment result or clinical recommendation. What this page should explain Key points How PRP is prepared What it is intended to do, and why preparation and indication matter. Procedure-related risks Possible pain, bruising, bleeding, infection and other procedure-related risks. Clinician review Why suitability and expected outcomes require review by a qualified clinician, with reference to local regulatory requirements. Research vs. established useThere is an important difference between studying a treatment and establishing that it is safe and effective for a particular purpose. Claims of breast enhancement should be assessed against appropriate clinical evidence for the precise procedure offered.What to askAsk what evidence supports the specific use, what the known risks are, and what regulatory requirements apply to that intended use in your jurisdiction. Further reading from the consolidated articleU.S. FDA — Dermal fillers and their approved usesU.S. FDA — Regenerative medicine and stem cell safety Questions PRP FAQs Is PRP proven for breast enlargement? PRP should not be marketed as a proven method of increasing breast size without robust evidence supporting that particular use. Effects depend on the specific indication and the available evidence. Is PRP safe because it uses my own blood? Using your own blood reduces some risks but does not remove them. Any procedure carries procedure-related risks such as pain, bruising, bleeding or infection, and suitability still requires clinical review. Education & Research Understanding Breast Enlargement: An Evidence-Aware Overview Before comparing treatments, it helps to understand what breast enlargement actually involves — and the difference between changing how the breasts look and changing the breast itself. Home/Education & Research/Understanding Breast Enlargement: An Evidence-Aware Overview “Breast enlargement” describes two very different things. One is a change in the look of the breasts — a bra, padding, posture or clothing. The other is a change in the breast itself — more glandular or fatty tissue, or a device placed inside it. Confusing the two is the single most common reason people spend money on something that cannot work.This page sets out the vocabulary, the biology and the framework used throughout the rest of the site, so that every treatment page and evidence verdict has a clear reference point. The core distinction Appearance vs. tissue Appearance only A correctly fitted bra, padding, push-up styles, inserts, styling and posture change how the chest looks immediately. They carry no medical risk, are fully reversible, and do not alter breast tissue. Real tissue or a device Fat transfer moves your own fat into the breast; implants place a prosthesis. Both are procedures with recovery, risk and cost. Only these routes add lasting volume without hormones. What the breast is made ofThe breast sits on the chest wall over the pectoral muscles. It contains glandular tissue (lobules and ducts that produce and carry milk), fibrous connective tissue that supports it, and fat. There is no muscle inside the breast — a point that explains why chest exercises firm the wall but do not enlarge the breast. Skin and suspensory ligaments give the breast its shape and are the structures that stretch with pregnancy, weight change and age.Breast size is therefore determined by how much glandular and fatty tissue sits on the chest, plus the skin envelope around it. Nothing applied to the surface of the skin can grow the tissue underneath.How breast tissue actually growsBreast development is driven mainly by hormones — above all oestrogen — during puberty, with further changes in pregnancy and breastfeeding. In adult life, breast volume mostly follows overall body fat, the hormonal cycle, pregnancy and age. The signal that builds breast tissue is internal and hormonal.This is why the only known routes to more tissue are hormonal stimulation (a medical matter, not a cosmetic one), fat transfer (your own fat, moved by a surgeon), and implants (a prosthesis). Creams, pills, massage, suction cups and devices have no established mechanism for adding breast tissue at all. A quick test: swelling or growth?If fullness fades within hours or days, it was fluid, swelling or a cycle effect — not growth.If it appears and disappears with your menstrual cycle, it is a normal cyclical change.If it follows weight gain, the fat changed — and that would happen without any product.Lasting added volume appears only after a procedure that places tissue or material in the breast, or after hormonal development. At a glance The four broad routes to more volume The four broad routes to more volume RouteWhat it isAdds lasting tissue?Nature CosmeticBras, padding, styling, postureNo — changes appearance onlyFree or low cost, reversible, no medical risk Fat transferYour own fat moved by liposuction and injectionYes — modest and variableMinimally invasive procedure with real risks ImplantsA saline or silicone device placed surgicallyYes — predictable volumeSurgery with long-term monitoring and revision risk HormonalMedically supervised hormone treatmentYes, in principleA medical treatment, not a cosmetic route; carries systemic risks Non-surgical injectables such as fillers, PRP and biostimulators do not belong on this list as reliable routes to lasting volume — see the evidence guide for why. How to use this website A clear path from curiosity to an informed decision Work through the information at your own pace. No decision about your body should ever be rushed by advertising. 01 Understand the biologyRead this page and the breast anatomy guide so that you can tell appearance changes from tissue changes. 02 Learn each optionWork through the non-surgical and surgical sections to understand intended effects, mechanisms and limitations. 03 Check the evidenceUse the evidence guide and research libraries to see what is proven, what is unproven and what to avoid. 04 Understand the risksReview candidacy, contraindications, complications and the warning signs that need medical attention. 05 Prepare for a clinicianTake written questions to a registered, appropriately qualified professional and compare more than one opinion. Educational information only — not medical adviceThis page explains concepts for general education. It cannot account for your health, anatomy or circumstances, and it does not recommend any treatment. Decisions about breast enlargement should be made with a qualified, registered clinician after proper assessment. Education & Research Breast Anatomy Explained: Tissue, Ligaments and Blood Supply Understanding the structures of the breast explains why some treatments can add volume, why sagging happens, and why injecting or operating carries the risks it does. Home/Education & Research/Breast Anatomy Explained: Tissue, Ligaments and Blood Supply The breast is not a simple sac of tissue. It is a layered structure whose behaviour — how it changes with weight and hormones, how it sags, and how it responds to surgery or injection — follows from what it is made of and how it is supplied with blood and nerve.Simplified educational schematic; not an operative or diagnostic diagram. Structures The layers and what each one does The layers and what each one does StructureWhat it isWhy it matters Skin & subcutaneous fatThe outer envelope and the fat immediately beneath itDetermines the covering of the breast and where surgery marks fall Glandular tissueLobules and ducts that produce and carry milkThe functional tissue; its proportion to fat varies greatly between people Fatty tissueAdipose tissue distributed around the glandular tissueA large part of breast volume; follows overall body fat and can be moved by fat transfer Cooper’s ligamentsFibrous bands anchoring the breast to the chest wall and skinSupport the breast; stretching with age, weight change and pregnancy contributes to sagging Pectoral musclesChest muscles lying under the breastThere is no muscle in the breast itself — so training builds the wall, not the breast Blood supplyArteries feeding the breast from several directionsCritical to fat-graft survival and to safe surgery; a blocked vessel by injected material can be catastrophic NervesSensory and autonomic nerves to breast and nippleTheir position explains why surgery and procedures can change nipple and skin sensation Lymph drainageVessels draining toward the axilla (armpit) and internal mammary chainRelevant to cancer detection and to interpreting injected material on imaging Why anatomy shapes every treatment decisionExisting tissue. A breast with little natural tissue cannot hide a large implant or supply much fat for reabsorption; a breast with a lot of tissue behaves differently again. This is why implant selection and fat-transfer volumes are individual decisions, not catalogue choices.Skin quality and laxity. Skin and the suspensory ligaments determine how well a breast holds its shape. Stretched skin after pregnancy or weight change is one reason a lift may be discussed alongside augmentation.Blood supply. Fat survives only where the tissue around it can supply blood. Poor blood supply is a central reason a proportion of transferred fat does not survive, and why large-volume grafting is unreliable. It is also why any injected material that obstructs a vessel is dangerous.Sensation and breastfeeding. Nerve pathways to the nipple pass through the breast. Depending on the technique, surgery and some procedures can affect nipple sensation or future breastfeeding, which is why these are discussed before consent. Anatomy is why “non-surgical” is not automatically “safe”The breast is a blood-rich, nerve-dense area that drains to the lymph nodes. Material injected into it can migrate, obstruct vessels, provoke inflammation and complicate cancer screening. That is the anatomical reason regulators advise against injecting fillers or silicone to enlarge the breasts — not merely a labelling matter. Putting it in contextThis page gives a general anatomical overview. Individual anatomy varies widely, and how any structure affects your own options can only be assessed in person by a qualified clinician. Education & Research Breast Enhancement Options Compared: Surgical vs Non-Surgical This comparison helps distinguish a procedure’s intended effect from claims made in advertising. It does not suggest that a non-surgical procedure is automatically safer than surgery. Home/Education & Research/Breast Enhancement Options Compared: Surgical vs Non-Surgical At a glance Intended effect, primary consideration and key limitation Intended effect, primary consideration and key limitation OptionPrimary considerationImportant limitation Dermal fillersProduct-specific approved indicationsNot FDA-approved for breast enlargement PRPEvidence for the particular intended useShould not be promoted as proven breast enlargement Threads & mono threadsProduct-specific aesthetic indicationsNot established substitutes for breast augmentation Sculptra / biostimulatorsProduct-specific authorised usesDo not assume suitability for breast-volume enhancement Stem-cell approachesEvidence and regulatory status of the exact productMany marketed regenerative uses remain unapproved or investigational Silicone breast implantsSurgical increase in breast volumeSurgery, implant-related risks and potential future procedures Fat transferUses the patient’s own fat for augmentationVariable fat retention and a limited, individualised result Choosing between options is not a matter of finding the “safest” label. It requires understanding your goals, your anatomy and health, the evidence for each intended effect, and the risks you are prepared to accept. A consultation with an appropriately qualified clinician is the appropriate way to reach an individualised view. Why the distinction mattersNot every treatment marketed as “non-surgical breast enlargement” has demonstrated a reliable increase in breast volume. Surgical and non-surgical approaches differ in their intended effect, their evidence base, their risks and their recovery requirements. Treating them as interchangeable can lead to unrealistic expectations.Intended outcomeSurgical augmentation is designed to increase breast volume or change breast shape. Some non-surgical treatments target skin quality or provide a different aesthetic effect rather than a meaningful increase in volume. Others are marketed for volume but lack robust supporting evidence for that specific use.Evidence and regulatory statusThe evidence base differs sharply. Dermal fillers are not approved for breast enlargement, and regulators advise against using them for this purpose. Regenerative and biostimulatory products require careful scrutiny of their evidence and regulatory status.Recovery and risk“Non-surgical” does not mean risk-free. Any procedure carries some risk, and the consequences of complications can differ substantially between approaches. Surgery carries surgical and implant-related risks and may involve future procedures.How to decideThe appropriate option depends on your health, anatomy, expectations and risk tolerance, and on the evidence for the intended treatment. That assessment should be made by an appropriately qualified clinician, not from advertising alone. Education & Research Breast Enlargement Safety: Candidacy, Risks and Warning Signs Safety is not a property of a treatment label; it is the balance of benefit, risk and suitability for one person. This page brings the safety points from every option into one place. Home/Education & Research/Breast Enlargement Safety: Candidacy, Risks and Warning Signs “Non-surgical” describes a method, not a risk level. A cream carries almost no medical risk but also does nothing; an injectable can be marketed as non-surgical and still cause serious harm; surgery carries the risks of any operation. Safety means matching the smallest effective intervention to your actual goal, after honest assessment. Candidacy Factors that shape whether a procedure is appropriate General health Medical conditions, medications and allergies can affect whether a procedure is suitable and how healing proceeds. Timing Pregnancy, breastfeeding and significant planned weight change all argue for waiting. Anatomy & tissue Existing tissue, skin quality and chest-wall proportions determine what is realistically achievable. Age Breasts may keep developing into the late teens and early twenties; most professional guidance advises against enlargement procedures for minors. Expectations Realistic expectations — and a willingness to accept that revision may be needed — are part of candidacy. Contraindications Active infection, certain uncontrolled conditions and pregnancy are typical reasons to postpone or decline a procedure. Risk by route What can go wrong, by option What can go wrong, by option RouteMain risksSeverity Bras, padding, stylingSkin irritation from adhesive productsVery low Creams and pillsAllergic reactions; undeclared or hormone-active ingredientsLow, but no benefit Suction / vacuum devicesBruising, broken vessels, skin damageLow to moderate Fat transferFat necrosis, oil cysts, calcification, infection, asymmetry; complications reported in about a quarter of cases in the largest reviewModerate External expansion + fat transferEverything above plus skin problems and rare serious events from prolonged device wearModerate Implants (surgery)Capsular contracture, rupture, ALCL, infection, sensation change, revision surgeryModerate to serious Injectable fillers in the breastNodules, migration, infection, imaging interference, difficulty of removal; not approved for this useHigh Liquid silicone / unknown injectablesDisfigurement, embolism, stroke or death; problems may appear years laterVery high Figures describe the groups studied and may not apply to any individual. See the evidence guide for the data behind the non-surgical rows. Warning signs — seek help promptlyFever, spreading redness, pus or worsening pain after any procedure — possible infection; contact your clinician the same day.Pale, bluish, dusky or dark skin, or blisters — may mean reduced blood supply; seek urgent care.Chest pain, breathlessness or collapse — possible blood clot; call emergency services.Sudden vision change, severe headache or weakness after an injection — possible blocked vessel; call emergency services.A new lump, hardness or skin change — have it examined and imaged. Suitability, risks and outcomes vary and require evaluation by an appropriately qualified clinician. 1–3: Credentials and experienceWhat are your qualifications and registration? Which specific breast procedures do you perform, and how often? Who will carry out my procedure and follow-up?4–6: The proposed treatmentWhat exactly are you recommending, and why? What are the approved indications for that product or procedure? What can it realistically achieve — and what can it not?7–8: Risks and alternativesWhat are the risks and possible complications, and how would they be managed? What alternatives exist, including doing nothing?9–10: Cost and aftercareWhat is the full cost, including any revision or follow-up? What aftercare and follow-up will I receive, and when should I seek medical attention? Further reading from the consolidated articleU.S. FDA — Dermal fillers and their approved usesU.S. FDA — Breast implantsAmerican Society of Plastic Surgeons — Questions to ask your plastic surgeon (https://www.plasticsurgery.org/cosmetic-procedures/breast-augmentation/questions) Choosing a qualified surgeonAdvertising is not a credential. Anyone can describe themselves as a “cosmetic surgeon”, and clinics may use the word “expert” freely. What can be verified is registration with a professional regulator, recognised surgical training, and membership of a relevant professional body. Verification How to check a surgeon before you commit These steps are cheap, quick and entirely reasonable to insist on. 01 Confirm registrationFind the surgeon on your national medical council or regulator and confirm the registration is current and unrestricted. 02 Confirm surgical trainingA surgeon performing breast surgery should hold recognised training in plastic or reconstructive surgery, not merely a short cosmetic course. 03 Check scope of practiceThe clinician should operate within their qualifications; ask directly who will perform each part of the procedure. 04 Check the operating settingAsk where the procedure is performed, who provides anaesthesia, and what arrangements exist for emergencies. 05 Ask for the plan in writingA reputable surgeon provides a written plan covering technique, risks, costs and revision policy — so you can think it over. Questions What to ask at the consultation What to ask at the consultation QuestionWhat a good answer looks like How many of these procedures do you personally perform each year?A specific number and a willingness to discuss outcomes, not evasion. What are your complication and revision rates?Honest acknowledgment that complications occur, with figures or a range, not a claim of zero. What would you do if I were unhappy with the result?A clear revision policy and costs, stated in advance. Which options are you not offering me, and why?A balanced comparison — including options that are less profitable or out of scope. How do you handle a problem after surgery?A named route for concerns, including out-of-hours arrangements. Can I take the written plan home before deciding?Yes, without pressure. A cooling-off period is normal and expected. Red flags that should end a consultationPressure to decide or pay a deposit the same day, or a “limited-time” discount.Guaranteed results, guaranteed symmetry, or claims of “no risk”.Vague or evasive answers about who performs the surgery and where.Reluctance to provide a written plan, quote or revision policy.Pushing an unapproved injectable, or refusing to name the exact product being offered.No discussion of alternatives, contraindications or what happens if things go wrong. Why a cooling-off period mattersCosmetic surgery decisions are permanent enough that reflection is part of good practice. Professional bodies such as the UK’s BAPRAS describe a consultation and cooling-off period before consent precisely because a rushed decision is a poor decision. If a clinic discourages taking time, that in itself is information. Questions Safety FAQs Is non-surgical always safer than surgery? No. A cream is low-risk but ineffective; unapproved breast filler is “non-surgical” yet linked to serious harm; surgery carries real but better-understood risks. Safety depends on the specific product, the indication and who performs it. How do I know if a clinic is safe? Check registration and credentials, insist on a written plan and revision policy, ask who performs the procedure and where, and treat pressure or guarantees as red flags. See choosing a surgeon. Are there signs I should not have a procedure at all? Yes. Active infection, pregnancy or breastfeeding, some uncontrolled medical conditions, and unrealistic expectations are typical reasons to postpone or decline. A good clinician will say so. Education & Research Glossary of Medical Terms Plain-language definitions of the terms you will meet on this site and in a consultation. Home/Education & Research/Glossary of Medical Terms Terms are arranged alphabetically. Definitions are deliberately short and non-promotional — enough to follow a consultation or a research abstract, not a substitute for clinical advice.autologous fat graftingThe transfer of a patient's own (autologous) fat from one part of the body to another; the scientific name for fat transfer.BIA-ALCLBreast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma — a rare lymphoma of the fluid or capsule around an implant, linked mainly to textured implants.BIA-SCCBreast implant-associated squamous cell carcinoma — a very rare cancer in the capsule around an implant.biostimulatorA broad category of injectable products intended to stimulate a tissue response such as collagen production, for selected approved indications.breast augmentationSurgery to increase breast size or change shape, using implants or, in selected cases, the patient's own fat.breast implantA medical device placed surgically to increase breast volume or restore shape, filled with saline (salt water) or silicone gel.breast implant illnessA term used for self-reported systemic symptoms such as fatigue, "brain fog", joint pain and rash attributed to implants; not an established diagnosis.breast reductionSurgery that removes breast tissue, fat and skin to reduce breast size and weight, often to relieve physical symptoms.capsular contractureTightening and hardening of the scar tissue capsule that naturally forms around an implant; a common reason for revision surgery.capsulectomySurgical removal of the scar capsule around a breast implant, sometimes performed at the same time as implant exchange or removal.cohesive gel implantA silicone implant whose gel holds together, so it tends to stay in shape even if the shell is cut; often called form-stable or "gummy bear".dermal fillerAn injectable product used for certain approved aesthetic indications; not approved for breast enlargement.explantationSurgical removal of breast implants, with or without replacement.external volume expansionPre-stretching the breast with a bra-like vacuum device worn for hours a day for weeks before fat transfer, aiming to improve fat survival.fat necrosisDeath of transferred fat cells that fail to establish a blood supply; may cause lumps, oil cysts or calcification visible on imaging.fat transferEnlargement or reshaping using the patient's own fat, removed by liposuction, processed and injected into the breast. Also called lipofilling or autologous fat grafting.haematomaA collection of blood (bruise) that can form after surgery and may require drainage.hyaluronic acid fillerA gel filler based on hyaluronic acid, used for approved aesthetic indications; its suitability for the breast is not established.implant ruptureLoss of integrity of a breast implant shell. A silicone rupture can be "silent", producing no symptoms, which is why screening is advised.inframammary foldThe natural crease under the breast; a common and well-hidden incision site for implant placement.lipofillingAnother name for fat transfer: injecting the patient's own fat, usually after liposuction, to add volume or refine shape.liquid siliconeInjectable silicone that is not an implant and must never be used to enlarge the breast; linked to disfigurement, embolism and death.mammographyX-ray imaging of the breast used for screening and diagnosis; implants, fat transfer and fillers can change its appearance.mastopexyA breast lift: reshaping and raising sagging breasts without deliberately adding volume.MRI screeningMagnetic resonance imaging used to check silicone implants for silent rupture, recommended by the FDA at intervals after placement.oil cystA pocket of liquefied fat that can form after fat necrosis following fat transfer; usually benign but may require assessment.periareolarAn approach or incision around the edge of the areola.poly-L-lactic acidA biodegradable collagen-stimulating injectable (for example Sculptra), licensed for specific facial indications, not for breast enlargement.PRPPlatelet-rich plasma: a preparation made by concentrating platelets from the patient's own blood, used in various regenerative procedures.ptosisSagging or drooping of the breast; its degree helps determine whether a lift is appropriate.revision surgeryAn operation to adjust, exchange, reposition or remove breast implants after a previous procedure.saline implantA breast implant filled with sterile salt water; if the shell leaks, the implant collapses and the fluid is absorbed or expelled.seromaA collection of fluid that can form after surgery or around an implant.silicone implantA breast implant filled with silicone gel, which tends to feel more like natural breast tissue and does not collapse if the shell leaks.subglandularPlacing a breast implant behind the breast tissue but in front of the pectoral muscle.submuscularPlacing a breast implant behind the pectoral muscle.transaxillaryAn approach to breast augmentation through an incision in the armpit (axilla). A note on terminologySome terms — such as “regenerative” or “non-surgical” — are used in marketing far more loosely than their technical meaning allows. Where that happens, this site explains the gap rather than repeating the claim. Continue reading Related education Education & Research Return to the full category guide. Every individual situation still requires assessment by an appropriately qualified clinician. Home/Education & Research/Frequently Asked Questions Questions about an individual optionRead the dedicated FAQs for fillers, PRP, fat transfer and augmentation and recovery. Common questions Breast enhancement FAQs Can breast size be increased without surgery? Some treatments are marketed for this purpose, but the evidence and regulatory status vary. Many non-surgical approaches have not been shown to reliably increase breast volume. A professional assessment is the appropriate way to establish what is realistic and which options, if any, are appropriate. What is the difference between silicone implants and injectable silicone? They are entirely different. Injectable silicone is a different product and should not be used as a substitute for a breast implant. Injectable silicone used for breast enhancement can cause serious, potentially permanent harm. How do I know which procedure is right for me? The appropriate option depends on your health, anatomy, expectations, risk tolerance and the evidence for the intended treatment. The decision should follow an assessment by an appropriately qualified clinician. Continue reading Related education Education & Research Return to the full category guide. Education & Research Breast Enlargement Research Library An independent reading guide to external research and patient information. These studies and source publications are not Quantum Health research. Home/Education & Research/Breast Enlargement Research Library External research, clearly attributedQuantum Health provides educational summaries, not original clinical research. Publication does not prove effectiveness. Read each source in context, check its date and jurisdiction, and distinguish a registered protocol from a completed review. PubMed study summaries · Search PMC records · Cochrane systematic reviews and protocols · U.S. FDA — regulator guidance · NHS — UK patient information · healthdirect — Australian health information · Cleveland Clinic — external patient education · American Society of Plastic Surgeons · British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons · British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons · StatPearls — NCBI Bookshelf clinical review · MedlinePlus — National Library of Medicine · Wikipedia — enlargement encyclopedia reference · Wikipedia — augmentation encyclopedia reference PubMed: topic-grouped study findingsThis page collects peer-reviewed research on breast enlargement — surgical and non-surgical — indexed in PubMed, the US National Library of Medicine’s database of biomedical literature. In October 2026 we searched PubMed using title and abstract terms covering breast augmentation, breast enlargement, fat transfer and autologous fat grafting, non-surgical enlargement, breast implants and breast fillers. Of 77 unique records retrieved, the most relevant are summarised here, grouped by topic, with a link to each original PubMed record.What the literature shows in brief: breast augmentation with implants remains one of the most frequently performed aesthetic operations worldwide, with predictable volume but real complication and revision rates. Autologous fat grafting is the best-supported route to lasting volume without an implant, but the gain is modest and complications occur in roughly a quarter of cases in the largest systematic review. External vacuum expansion has produced true tissue growth in small studies, but demands weeks of daily device wear. Injectable fillers are not approved for breast enlargement, and published case series document serious complications. Creams, pills and most devices have no credible supporting trials. How this page was compiledSearches were run on PubMed (National Library of Medicine, USA) in October 2026 using title/abstract terms: “breast augmentation”, “breast enlargement”, (“fat transfer” OR “autologous fat grafting” OR “fat grafting”) AND breast augmentation, (“non-surgical” OR filler OR PRP OR “platelet-rich plasma”) AND breast enlargement, and breast implants AND (augmentation OR enlargement). 77 unique records were retrieved; the studies most relevant to breast enlargement are summarised below. Summaries use abstract-level data — consult the full article and current guidelines before drawing clinical conclusions. Inclusion here is not an endorsement of any study or treatment. Evidence at a glance The headline findings, by question Each row links to the PubMed record behind the finding. The headline findings, by question QuestionWhat the published evidence showsKey studies Does fat transfer enlarge breasts?Yes — modestly. The largest systematic review (35 studies, 3,757 women) reported an average 58% fat retention from about 300 mL injected per breast — roughly one cup — with a 27.8% overall complication rate and 92% average patient satisfaction.Seth 2024 (PMID 37166041) Is fat transfer better than implants?The only randomised trial identified found implants gave more evident and durable augmentation (87.5% vs 70% “excellent” aesthetic outcomes), while fat grafting produced more natural-looking results and better correction of chest-wall deformity.Gentile 2026 (PMID 40908320) Can a vacuum device enlarge breasts without surgery?A 2000 study reported a stable 55% average size increase after 10 weeks of daily external expansion (10–12 h/day); MRI confirmed growth of fat and fibroglandular tissue. Evidence remains limited and largely developer-led.Khouri 2000 (PMID 10845308); Kardorff 2004 (PMID 16285326) Do breast fillers work — and are they safe?Hyaluronic acid gel was briefly authorised for breast use in Europe (2008), then withdrawn worldwide after side effects. A 31-patient complication series found 88.9% of conservatively treated aquafilling cases needed reoperation. Regulators advise against fillers for breast enlargement.Siebert 2014 (PMID 24507861); Gierej 2023 (PMID 37721627); Jeyaratnam 2021 (PMID 34849315) How often do implants need revision?Reported revision rates after primary augmentation are as high as 36%, most commonly for capsular contracture, implant malposition and ptosis of the ageing breast.Denney 2021 (PMID 34121945) Is “breast implant illness” established?Systemic symptoms attributed to implants are widely reported, but a 2024 Danish review notes the correlation with implants is not established, evidence is limited, and it is not a recognised diagnosis.Borhani-Khomani 2024 (PMID 38808767) How common is augmentation worldwide?ISAPS 14-year global data show breast augmentation consistently among the top five surgical aesthetic procedures. Implant removal has been the fastest-growing procedure since 2015 (+46.3% over five years).Triana 2024 (PMID 39103642) Study figures describe the groups studied and may not apply to any individual. Evidence and regulatory positions change — check the linked records and current regulator guidance before acting. Fat transfer (autologous fat grafting)Fat transfer removes fat by liposuction from another body area and injects it into the breast. It is the best-documented route to real, lasting volume without an implant — but the gain is modest, and the evidence base, while growing, is still dominated by retrospective series rather than controlled trials. Fat transfer studies What fat-grafting research reports What fat-grafting research reports StudyDesignWhat it found Seth I, et al. 2024 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 37166041)Systematic review: 35 studies, 3,757 womenAverage 300 mL injected per breast; 58% volume retention (range 44–83%); 27.8% overall complication rate, fat necrosis the most common (43.7% of complications); radiologic fat necrosis 9.4%, calcification 1.2%; 92% average satisfaction at one year. Gentile P. 2026 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 40908320)Randomised open-label trial: 95 implants vs 90 lipofilling87.5% of implant patients vs 70% of lipofilling patients had excellent aesthetic outcomes at 12 months. Implant results were significantly more durable; lipofilling results were judged more natural and improved pectus excavatum. Both were safe and effective. Voglimacci M, et al. 2015 — Aesthetic Surg J (PMID 25908697)Systematic review: 42 articlesEvidence mostly low level (one level-2 study). Two cancers among 2,023 patients (0.09%) with insufficient follow-up for long-term conclusions. Concludes registries with proper follow-up are needed. Leopardi D, et al. 2014 — ANZ J Surg (PMID 23656507)Systematic review vs implant comparatorsNo comparative studies were found. Fat necrosis, cysts and lumps were the most common complications; reabsorption occurs mainly in the first 12 months; efficacy could not be determined from the available evidence. Hivernaud V, et al. 2015 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 26085223)Technique reviewHigh resorption remains the central problem of large-volume grafting; refinements in harvesting and graft preparation aim to improve fat viability and long-term success. Coleman SR, Saboeiro AP. 2015 — Clin Plast Surg (PMID 26116935)Technique reviewThe 2009 ASPS Fat Graft Task Force concluded fat grafting may be considered for breast augmentation, with results dependent on technique and surgeon expertise. Finzi E. 2003 — Dermatol Surg (PMID 12930335)Retrospective record reviewBreast enlargement occurred in 43% of patients after tumescent liposuction of other body areas; 30% gained one cup size or more — an incidental, redistribution-based effect. Seth I, et al. 2023 — Gland Surg (PMID 36761486)Method paper: hybrid augmentationProposes a preoperative formula to estimate fat-graft volume when combining implants with lipofilling (hybrid breast augmentation). Non-surgical enlargement: external expansionExternal vacuum expansion devices (bra-like systems worn for hours a day) aim to grow tissue through controlled mechanical stretch. Small studies report measurable growth; the regimens are demanding, and critics have questioned measurement consistency. Expansion studies External expansion: the published record External expansion: the published record StudyDesignWhat it found Khouri RK, et al. 2000 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 10845308)Single-group study: 17 women (12 completed)A brassiere-like system applying 20 mmHg per breast, 10–12 h/day for 10 weeks: peak increase 98%; after recoil, a stable long-term increase of 55% (range 15–115%). MRI confirmed proportionate growth of adipose and fibroglandular tissue. No adverse events recorded. Kardorff B, et al. 2004 — JDDG (PMID 16285326)German case report using the same protocolChest circumference at the nipple level remained 4 cm above baseline at three months after oedema resolved. Side effects were limited to transient irritant contact dermatitis and folliculitis. He Y, et al. 2017 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 28350663)Preclinical/technique studyCombining minimally invasive tissue dissection with external volume expansion generated far more adipose tissue than expansion alone, mediated by release of cell-contact inhibition. Tebbetts JB. 2001 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 11379562)Critical reviewArgued that claimed non-surgical enlargement largely reflects measurement variability and soft-tissue change rather than reliable true tissue growth — a caution against overstating the early expansion data. Uyulmaz S, et al. 2020 — Praxis (PMID 33109001)Clinical reviewReviews implant-free cosmetic augmentation: mastopexy for optical lift and lipofilling for volume; large-volume or high-goal augmentation with fat alone remains limited. Fillers and injectable productsNo injectable filler is approved for breast enlargement by major regulators. The published literature documents what happens when fillers are used in the breast: product withdrawal, complication series and reoperation. Filler safety evidence What the filler studies report What the filler studies report StudyDesignWhat it found Siebert T, et al. 2014 — Ann Chir Plast Esthet (PMID 24507861)Literature review (Macrolane)Hyaluronic acid gel (Macrolane) received European authorisation for breast augmentation in 2008, then was withdrawn from the worldwide breast-augmentation market after numerous side-effect controversies. Gierej P, et al. 2023 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 37721627)Observational cohort: 31 women with aquafilling-gel complications88.9% of patients treated conservatively required reoperation, vs 22.7% after radical surgery. Needle aspiration was ineffective and associated with infection (75% positive cultures). More filler injected correlated with more symptoms. Jeyaratnam S, Joethy J. 2021 — PRS Global Open (PMID 34849315)Case-based reviewDocuments the dangers of filler breast augmentation, consistent with regulator advice against the practice. Implant augmentation: outcomes, complications and revisionImplant surgery has the largest evidence base of any augmentation method. The studies below cover complication prevention, revision burden, device history, imaging and patient-reported systemic symptoms. Implant studies Implant augmentation: the study data Implant augmentation: the study data StudyDesignWhat it found Denney BD, et al. 2021 — Semin Plast Surg (PMID 34121945)ReviewRevision rates after primary augmentation remain as high as 36%; the commonest causes are capsular contracture, implant malposition and ptosis of the ageing breast. Nava MB, et al. 2017 — Gland Surg (PMID 28497025)Evidence reviewNo high-level evidence identifies a single best technique or implant; complication reduction follows established surgical principles rather than device fashion. Nahabedian MY. 2019 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 31246764)Review of form-stable implantsReviews diagnosis and management of complications with modern cohesive-gel implants; no implant lasts forever, though devices remain safe and effective per clinical and epidemiologic studies. Kaoutzanis C, et al. 2019 — Semin Plast Surg (PMID 31632203)Historical reviewTraces implant evolution since 1962, including the silicone-gel controversies, and how successive generations improved safety and aesthetics. Correia-Sá I, et al. 2013 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 23943050)Case report with histologyPIP implants showed increased rupture and leakage risk; documents clinical, histologic and microbiologic findings after rupture, including siliconoma and lymph-node involvement. Monstrey S, et al. 2004 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 15108875)Case series: 13 patientsTrilucent (soybean-oil-filled) implants failed because of lipid-oxidation metabolites; UK and Belgian authorities advised removal — a documented device-withdrawal precedent. Simádo TS. 2021 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 33885442)Clinical algorithmGalactorrhea and galactocele after breast augmentation: a diagnosis and treatment algorithm. Green LA, et al. 2018 — Clin Imaging (PMID 28918365)Imaging reviewBreast-cancer screening must continue after augmentation; radiologists need familiarity with surgical techniques, implant appearances and MRI findings. Faguy K. 2018 — Radiol Technol (PMID 29793920)Imaging reviewCatalogues adverse effects and imaging appearances of breast implants for technologists and radiologists. Borhani-Khomani K, et al. 2024 — Ugeskr Læger (PMID 38808767)Danish reviewSelf-reported systemic symptoms attributed to implants (“breast implant illness”): the correlation is not established, evidence is limited, and the condition is not currently a recognised diagnosis. Luan J. 2023 — Clin Plast Surg (PMID 36396254)Technique reviewEndoscopic-assisted transaxillary augmentation: the axillary approach remains preferred by many patients in Asia; endoscopy improves control and stability of the result. Bekeny JC, et al. 2020 — Gland Surg (PMID 32775269)Review (transfeminine augmentation)Augmentation for transfeminine patients is technically similar to that for cisgender peers, with equivalent complication rates and documented quality-of-life benefits. Holst-Albrechtsen S, et al. 2018 — Ugeskr Læger (PMID 29886889)Clinical studyPost-operative infections after cosmetic surgery abroad (“cosmetic tourism”) — treatment abroad carries identifiable infection risk. Global trends and contemporary benchmarksLarge registry analyses show how often augmentation is performed, how preferences are shifting, and where the field is heading. Trends What the registry and benchmark studies report What the registry and benchmark studies report StudyDesignWhat it found Triana L, et al. 2024 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 39103642)ISAPS global statistics, 2010–202334.9 million aesthetic procedures worldwide in 2023. Breast augmentation has remained consistently in the top five surgical procedures for 14 years, with a first decline in the most recent year; implant removal is the fastest-growing procedure since 2015 (+46.3% over five years). Glicksman CA. 2026 — Clin Plast Surg (PMID 41826039)Benchmarks reviewContemporary benchmarks in breast augmentation surgery — current reference points for planning and outcomes. Lhuaire M, et al. 2019 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 31764702)Technique paperMinimally invasive inframammary breast augmentation — approaches aimed at smaller, hidden incisions. Lin Y, et al. 2022 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 33403418)Anthropometric studyBody and breast measurements in augmentation planning — objective sizing data supporting implant selection. Questions About this research page What is PubMed, and why use it? PubMed is the US National Library of Medicine’s free index of biomedical literature, covering thousands of peer-reviewed journals. Searching it gives a structured, reproducible view of what has actually been studied — rather than what is advertised. Does listing a study mean we recommend its findings? No. Listing means the study is part of the published evidence base. Individual studies vary in quality — a small case report carries far less weight than a systematic review or randomised trial. Nothing on this page is a recommendation for any individual. Why do study findings sometimes disagree? Different designs, patient groups, surgical techniques, measurement methods and eras produce different results. Where the Cochrane evidence runs outCochrane has published no systematic review of cosmetic breast augmentation as a procedure — no review of augmentation techniques, implant placement planes, satisfaction after cosmetic surgery, or long-term outcomes in women who had implants for enlargement rather than reconstruction. The completed reviews here were written for breast reduction and post-mastectomy reconstruction; their findings are evidence about those settings, not direct evidence about augmentation for cosmetic purposes.There is also no Cochrane review of fat transfer or autologous fat grafting for cosmetic breast enlargement (the reconstruction protocol was withdrawn in 2021), none of silicone gel implants used for cosmetic purposes, none of breast uplift (mastopexy), none of gynaecomastia surgery in men, and none of the non-surgical options discussed elsewhere on this site — fillers, platelet-rich plasma, threads or biostimulators. Absence of a Cochrane review does not mean a treatment works or does not work; it means the question has not been systematically synthesised at this level, and other evidence must be weighed instead. British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic SurgeonsThis page works through the patient guide published by the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons (BAPRAS) — the four-part guide to breast augmentation (bilateral breast augmentation, or BBA): what the operation is, how to choose a surgeon, implant techniques, the complications that can occur and the long-term consequences. Every part is summarised here and linked to the original, so the current wording can always be checked at source.BAPRAS describes breast enlargement as a potentially life-enhancing procedure — but also as a big decision: major surgery with potential risks, and a result that cannot be guaranteed. The guide was edited by Lee Martin and Emma de Sousa, with contributions from Julie Doughty, Paul Harris, Mark Henley, Nigel Mercer, Charles Nduka, Mary O’Brien, Caroline Payne and Ruth Waters, and was last updated in 2021. A printed copy of the guide is available from the BAPRAS secretariat, and a PDF is published alongside the online version.This summary is educational. It does not replace the discussion you should have with your own surgeon, and it does not constitute medical advice or a recommendation of any procedure, surgeon or clinic.
