What this page is — and is notThis is a condensed, section-by-section summary of BAPRAS patient information written for people considering breast enlargement in the United Kingdom. Figures such as complication frequencies are those published in the guide; UK practice, funding rules and professional registers differ between countries, so local standards still apply wherever a procedure is performed.Nothing here is a personal assessment of suitability. That can only be done in a consultation with a qualified, registered surgeon who examines you. What breast augmentation isBreast augmentation (bilateral breast augmentation or BBA) is an operation to enlarge the breasts, usually by inserting an implant beneath the breast to make it look larger. It can enlarge breasts that have always been small, and it can also fill out breasts that used to be larger — for example breasts that have emptied out after pregnancy. The procedure reshapes breasts to some extent and can be used to correct breasts that are of unequal size.An alternative to enlargement with an implant is fat transfer, sometimes called lipomodelling, lipofilling or fat grafting: fat taken from elsewhere on the body is injected into the breast area. Fat transfer may be appropriate for a few people but is not suitable for all, often requires more than one episode of surgery, and can also be combined with an implant augmentation.Patients who have breast augmentation tend to be pleased with the results, but the guide is explicit that expectations must be realistic. You need to understand what can and cannot be achieved, the limitations of surgery, and the long-term consequences of having breast implants. Next steps Getting to a decision The BAPRAS guide sets out a deliberate, unhurried path from first enquiry to the operating table. 01 Find a surgeonYour GP may be able to suggest surgeons locally, or you can approach a private hospital or clinic directly. If you do, make sure your initial consultation is with the surgeon who will actually do the operation. Your surgeon will normally seek permission to write to your GP afterwards. 02 Attend a full consultationYou will be asked what is bothering you about your breasts and what you expect from surgery, must share your full medical history, and will be examined with measurements taken. Discussion follows about implant shapes, possible sizes and the position of the pockets behind your existing breast tissue. A consultation fee is normal. 03 See the likely resultSome surgeons use implant sizers in a bra, others 3D photography. This is only a guide — the same implant can look very different in different people. You should be told about the operation, the expected outcome and the possible risks and complications. 04 Take the cooling-off periodYou should be given a cooling-off period of at least two weeks before surgery and offered a second consultation. You should not feel rushed into surgery — if you are, walk away. Why there is a cooling-off periodBreast augmentation is a lifetime commitment and must not be considered a one-stop permanent solution. You need to be making the appropriate choice and understand all the implications of the surgery you are considering — including that you will need revision surgery as the years go by, and that you must be prepared personally and financially for this.Nobody needs an urgent breast augmentation. If you are not offered a cooling-off period, or you are put under pressure to proceed, the guide’s advice is simple: walk away. Checks, costs and funding Before you commit Before you commit TopicWhat the BAPRAS guide says Checking your surgeonAll surgeons should be listed with the General Medical Council (GMC). Check the register at gmc-uk.org using “Check a doctor’s registration status”. Under “Status” they should be listed as “Registered with a license to practise; this doctor is on the specialist register”. Surgeons may also be registered with the Association of Breast Surgery (ABS), BAAPS and/or BAPRAS — members of these organisations hold a standard set of recognised qualifications. It is perfectly reasonable to ask about a surgeon’s experience and qualifications. Internet searchesInformation found through search engines may be promotional in nature; some surgeons and services pay for their listing. A prominent listing is a measure of marketing ability, not of service quality. CostAn approximate cost should be obtainable from your local private hospital or the surgeon’s secretary before your consultation, and you should expect to pay a fee for the consultation itself. After your consultation(s), if you plan to go ahead, you should be given a written quote for the planned care. Deposits and inducementsAvoid any deal asking for a non-refundable deposit, and do not accept a financial inducement or time-limited deal — even offering to refund the consultation fee if you proceed with surgery is considered an inducement and is against GMC guidance. Package pricesIt is appropriate to be offered a package covering the whole process and the cost of treating any complications arising in the initial weeks after surgery. You should be told exactly what the package includes. The cheapest deal may not be the best: cosmetic surgery is a significant financial commitment, and you will need to pay for further surgery in the future. NHS fundingCosmetic breast augmentation is not available on the NHS, so you will normally consult and pay privately. Exceptional circumstances can include very uneven breasts (a significant difference in size), having no breasts, or treatment as part of a breast reconstruction care plan — your GP can explain the rules in your area. Surgery abroadIf you go abroad for breast augmentation, be aware that on return to the UK only emergency complications will be dealt with by the NHS. Summarised from the BAPRAS patient guide. Cosmetic-surgery funding, regulation and professional registers differ between countries — verify the current position in your own jurisdiction. Implant techniquesBreast enlargement involves placing an implant under the breast tissue to increase the size and shape of the breast. Implants are usually inserted through an incision under the breast at the crease, but they can also be placed through an incision in the armpit or around the nipple.Behind the breast (sub-glandular)Placing the implant behind the breast, on top of the chest wall muscle, is considered the simplest of the available enlargement procedures and is less likely to cause significant discomfort. This route is also effective for patients with some drooping of the breasts.Behind the muscle (sub-muscular)Placing the implant behind the breast muscle gives more padding or coverage for the implant. This can help slender patients and those with very little breast tissue, because it reduces the chances of being able to feel or see the implant under the breast tissue.Dual plane augmentationSurgeons often combine the two routes, placing the implant partly behind the breast and partly behind the muscle, to try to give the benefits of both — this is called a dual plane augmentation. If implants are inserted behind the muscle they are likely to move when the muscle contracts; this is called animation and is normal. Your surgeon will advise which placement is appropriate for you. What the operation involvesBefore and after photographs should be taken for your clinical record, to help you and your surgeon plan the operation and assess the result. Your face is not included and you will be asked for consent; if your surgeon wants to use the images for teaching or publication, they must ask for specific additional consent.Breast enlargement surgery takes about one-and-a-half hours and is usually done under general anaesthetic. You may be able to go home the same day, but many patients spend one night in hospital. Postoperative pain should be well controlled: your chest may feel tight and your breasts and ribs may be tender. You will be mobile from day one and should be back to full exercise within six weeks, with one to two weeks off work recommended.At first the breasts may look high and the skin tight; this tends to settle over the first six weeks, but the long-term result takes three to four months as a more natural shape emerges. Most patients are pleased with their surgery, though some find the new shape difficult to get used to. Scars are typically quite red for the first six weeks, change to purple over the next three months and then fade to white. Most patients form good-quality scars, but abnormal scarring can occur. Implant techniques Choosing the implant Choosing the implant DecisionWhat the BAPRAS guide says Fill materialThe outer shell of all implants is made of silicone, and some have an additional polyurethane coating. The shell is filled with either silicone gel or saline. Implants have been used since the 1960s and the evidence suggests they are safe. Most patients are offered silicone gel-filled implants — they tend to feel the most natural, come in a range of shapes and are durable. Saline implants feel less natural, folds or ripples may be more visible, and they carry a risk of deflation. All other filler materials have been withdrawn for use in the UK. Ask your surgeon exactly which type and manufacturer will be used, and why. SizeImplants are supplied by volume, and it is not possible to guarantee a cup size. Your surgeon assesses your chest wall, your existing breast tissue and how much skin is available, then indicates an appropriate range — your own view matters, because in most patients a range of sizes could be used. The larger the implant and the slimmer you are, the less natural the result; an implant out of proportion with your frame is more likely to cause complications such as drooping, stretching of the breast tissue and being more easily felt. ShapeImplants are round or teardrop (anatomical). Round implants give more volume at the top of the breast and are as wide as they are tall. With teardrop implants the width and height can be chosen separately, giving more control of the eventual shape. Both come in varying degrees of projection; your surgeon discusses the best shape for your frame and desired outcome. TextureSurfaces are smooth or textured, in degrees from very fine to coarse; some implants have a foamy polyurethane coating. Texturing exists to reduce capsular contracture (evidence is strongest when the implant is placed in front of the muscle) and to reduce unwanted movement or rotation — so anatomical implants tend to be textured, while rotation of a round implant is not noticeable. A textured surface is linked to the uncommon BIA-ALCL; smooth implants currently have no such link. Smooth implants are almost always round, move within the breast and take several months to settle, and can slip sideways (lateral displacement) or drop below the crease (bottoming out). The choice is not straightforward — your surgeon should help decide. Silicone safetyImplants are made from medical-grade silicone. Small quantities of silicone can be taken up by the body and found in breast tissue and sometimes the armpit lymph glands; occasionally the body forms inflammation and extra tissue around silicone deposits (silicone granuloma). If the shell fails, the gel often keeps its shape and the appearance may not change — ruptures are frequently discovered by accident while investigating another breast problem, though they can cause lumpiness or a change in shape. A confirmed rupture is treated by removal of the implants, with replacement possible at the same or a later operation. There is no association between breast augmentation and breast cancer. The three most important decisions are implant size, shape and placement. Summarised from the BAPRAS implant techniques guide. What complications can occur?All operations are associated with risks. Serious complications are uncommon with breast augmentation, occurring in less than 1 in 100 operations. The figures below are those published in the BAPRAS guide. Reported frequencies Risks and how often they occur Risks and how often they occur ComplicationWhat the BAPRAS guide says Serious complications overallUncommon — less than 1 in 100 breast augmentation operations. Bleeding (haematoma)Less than 1 in 100. Usually immediately after surgery, occasionally up to two weeks later. The breast becomes very swollen and tight and you return to theatre to have the blood removed and the bleeding stopped; the implant can be retained. Expect an extra night in hospital and more bruising than usual. Haematoma can increase the risk of later capsular contracture. InfectionLess than 1 in 1000. Usually apparent over the first two or three weeks: swelling, tenderness, redness, wound discharge and a raised temperature. Antibiotics sometimes settle a mild infection, but most established infections around the implant require removal — a new implant cannot be inserted immediately, and three to six months should pass before re-insertion. Your package price should cover treatment of bleeding or infection. Capsular contractureThe body forms a scar capsule around every implant; when it contracts the breast feels firmer, and may become round or tender. Noticeable firmness occurs in up to 1 in 10 of all breast augmentations, but most of those patients do not need revision surgery. Options include living with it (safe), releasing the capsule (capsulotomy) or removing it (capsulectomy) with a new implant — but scar tissue can return in at least half of people having secondary surgery. Capsular contracture is the most common reason for re-operation, and once it has happened it is likely to recur in 1 in 2 cases. Re-operation for any reasonAbout 1% (1 in 100) per year — so after 10 years, about 10 in every 100 women will have had more surgery. Changes in sensationSome alteration of sensation is usual, most often numbness and oversensitivity of the nipples. Oversensitivity gradually settles, usually over several months. Around 1 in 5 patients have a reduction in nipple sensation; recovery can take up to 12 months, and 1 in 10 patients have some permanent numbness. Feeling or seeing the implantIt is common to feel the implant, especially in slim patients or those with little breast tissue; this is an inevitable consequence of the operation and does not improve with time. Ripples or folds may become visible leaning forwards. Small amounts of your own fat can be injected (lipomodelling) to improve the situation in some patients. A marked crease can be a sign of capsular contracture. Implant failure (rupture)The shell can eventually fail. The American Core study (FDA update, 2011) found 1 in 10 implants had ruptured at 10 years, and it is estimated half of all breast implants may rupture by 15 years. Rupture is often contained within the body’s own capsule (silent rupture) and does not appear harmful; some patients notice a change in size, shape or consistency, a lump or swelling. A scan is usually performed and, if rupture is suggested, removal and exchange is advised. There is no universally agreed replacement schedule, and exchange before ten years is unusual — if you have noticed no change, no regular follow-up or scans are needed. AsymmetrySome asymmetry between breasts is normal and perfect symmetry is not an achievable goal; asymmetry may appear more pronounced after surgery. A larger implant in the smaller breast improves the volume difference only, not other differences such as nipple position. Implants can also settle differently in their pockets. Wide cleavageImplants are positioned centrally behind the nipples and will not improve a naturally wide cleavage — with sub-muscular placement the cleavage can even appear wider. Breasts and implants falling to the sides when you lie down is normal. Stretch marks and veinsStretch marks may develop after surgery, especially with larger implants, and veins may become more noticeable on the breast surface. Ptosis (sagging)Breasts will sag with time because augmented breasts are larger and heavier — the larger the implant, the more the breast will droop. They may also “bottom out”, meaning the implant sits lower, below the nipple rather than above it. Pregnancy and breastfeedingImplants do not interfere with the ability to breastfeed. There is some evidence that the amount of milk produced by some women with implants is reduced, and no evidence of increased illness in children of women with silicone gel implants. Pregnancy and breastfeeding may adversely affect the shape of the breast. Other reasons for re-operationSome patients choose re-augmentation with larger implants as time goes by; augmented breasts change shape with time, pregnancy and weight fluctuation; teardrop-shaped implants can rotate behind the breast (usually rotating back by themselves or being gently pushed back, but repeated rotation needs re-operation, especially with large implants correcting droop); and intermittent swelling around an implant may lead to scans, further tests or implant replacement. Who pays for future treatmentMany of these long-term problems will not be covered by the package bought at the time of surgery, and you should not expect the NHS to provide future treatment. You must be prepared to pay for consultations, scans and further surgery if needed. Frequency figures are those published in the BAPRAS patient guide (updated 2021) and describe breast augmentation generally; individual risk depends on your anatomy, the technique used and your health. Breast Implant Associated Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (BIA-ALCL)Since 2016, anaplastic large cell lymphoma in association with breast implants has been recognised by the World Health Organization. The risk is small. It is not a breast cancer but a type of cancer associated with the scar tissue (capsule) the body lays down around an implant. Cases have occurred between 2 and 28 years after implant insertion, with an average of 8 years, and it most likely presents as swelling around the implant (a seroma) causing an increase in breast size. It can usually be treated successfully by removing the implant and the surrounding capsule.Because it is uncommon, international organisations share data on the condition. Most cases worldwide have occurred in women with textured breast implants, with higher numbers where the texture is coarser — so ask your surgeon for the most up-to-date recommendations. Breast implants continue to hold safety approval from government organisations such as the UK MHRA and the USA FDA and remain used in breast reconstruction after cancer worldwide.Breast Implant Illness (BII)Breast Implant Illness is a term used by some patients who experience symptoms they feel are connected to their silicone implants — tiredness, “brain fog”, joint aches, immune-related symptoms, sleep disturbance, depression, hormonal issues, headaches, hair loss, chills, rash and neurological issues. BII is not a medical diagnosis, there is no proven association with breast implants, and there is currently no scientific evidence confirming the proposed link or any diagnostic test for the condition; research continues. Some patients report improvement after implant removal, but not all do. The UK government guidance on BII symptoms and the FDA’s breast-implant risk pages are referenced in the guide. Long-term consequences and alternativesMammography and screeningImplants push your natural breasts forward and do not make it harder to examine your breasts for lumps, but they do interfere with mammography: X-rays cannot pass through the implant, so some breast tissue is obscured. UK breast screening starts at age 50. If you are called for a screening mammogram you must tell the service you have implants — they may scan you at a different centre and take special views. The more of your total breast volume that is implant, the greater the problem, so a breast augmentation reduces the sensitivity of a future mammogram. Some patients pay privately for MRI screening instead to avoid these issues.Myths and routine replacementIt is not unsafe to sunbathe or to fly in an aeroplane with implants — neither presents a problem. There is no need to massage breast implants, and this is not recommended with modern textured-surface implants. Routine replacement after a specified time is not recommended: replacement is advised only if you are unhappy with the appearance or have developed a problem.Alternatives: lipofilling and breast upliftThe only alternative surgical technique to enlarge the breast is lipofilling (fat transfer): fat is removed by liposuction from the hips, thighs or tummy and injected into the breast area. Only a relatively small amount can be injected, so multiple operations are usually needed for a worthwhile effect; some fat is absorbed in the first weeks, but fat lasting beyond that brings permanent enlargement. It is more gradual than implant surgery and avoids an implant, but the surgeon cannot be sure how effective it will be and results are variable. Your own fat is the only substance that can be safely injected into the breast — other materials have been tried and withdrawn. Do not allow anyone to inject anything other than your own fat.If you are bothered by droopiness but happy with your breast size, you do not need an augmentation — you may be offered a breast uplift (mastopexy), which lifts the nipple and breast tissue and tightens the skin, with incisions around the areola and possibly vertically and under the breast. Scarring is more obvious than with augmentation alone and no implant is used, but uplifted breasts tend to droop again with time and gravity, and often seem smaller afterwards despite little or no tissue removal. Mild droopiness can be improved by augmentation alone; where both volume loss and droopiness are a problem, augmentation and mastopexy may be discussed as one operation or in two stages — usually best done one at a time, though sometimes performed together after careful planning and counselling, with results that are not always entirely predictable in size and shape.Breast Implant RegistryIn the UK there is a national Breast and Cosmetic Implant Registry, administered by NHS Digital, recording every implant placed or removed with patient details, the organisation and the surgeon. Its main aim is to trace and inform affected patients if a failed implant is ever recalled, and to identify possible trends and complications relating to specific implants. Entry requires your consent, and you are strongly recommended to agree to the register if you have implant-based surgery — for your own protection and that of others. Quick answers Questions the BAPRAS guide answers Can my surgeon guarantee a cup size? No. Implants are supplied by volume and it is not possible to guarantee a cup size. Your surgeon assesses your chest wall, existing breast tissue and available skin, then indicates an appropriate range of sizes — in most patients a range could be used, and your own preference decides where in that range to sit. Do breast implants have to be replaced after a set number of years? No. There is no universally agreed replacement schedule, and exchange before ten years is unusual. If you have noticed no change you do not need regular follow-up or scans. You should still be prepared — personally and financially — for further surgery at some point, since about 1% of patients have a re-operation each year. Is breast enlargement available on the NHS? Cosmetically, no — you would consult and pay as a private patient. Exceptions include very uneven breasts, having no breasts, or treatment within a reconstruction care plan. If you have surgery abroad, only emergency complications will be treated by the NHS on your return. What exactly is the cooling-off period? At least two weeks between your decision and surgery, plus an offer of a second consultation beforehand. Nobody needs an urgent breast augmentation: if you are pressured to proceed or offered no cooling-off period, walk away. Are silicone implants safe? Implants are made from medical-grade silicone and have been used since the 1960s; the evidence suggests they are safe, and there is no association between breast augmentation and breast cancer. Rupture remains possible (about 1 in 10 at 10 years) and is usually treated by removal and exchange. Rare risks such as BIA-ALCL, and the symptoms described as breast implant illness, are covered above. What is the alternative to an implant? Lipofilling — transferring your own fat by liposuction and injection. It avoids an implant but usually needs several operations for a worthwhile effect, gives a gradual result and is variable. Your own fat is the only substance that should ever be injected into the breast. recovery can take up to 12 months, but 1 in 10 patients will have some permanent numbness.Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021) PalpabilityIt is common to be able to feel the implant, especially in slim patients or those with little breast tissue; this is an inevitable consequence of the operation and will not improve with time.Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021) Implant ruptureThe American Core study suggested 1 in 10 implants had ruptured at 10 years and half of all implants may rupture by 15 years; many ruptures are silent and contained within the capsule, but a symptomatic rupture should be investigated and the implant removed.Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021) Replacement scheduleThere is no universally agreed replacement schedule for breast implants and it is unusual to need exchange before ten years; routine replacement after a specified time is not recommended.Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021) BIA-ALCLBIA-ALCL is a rare cancer of the implant capsule recognised by the WHO, occurring 2 to 28 years after insertion (average 8 years), usually presenting as swelling around the implant, most often with textured implants — especially coarser textures — and usually treated by removing the implant and capsule.Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021) Breast Implant IllnessBreast Implant Illness is a term some patients use for symptoms including tiredness, brain fog, joint aches and others; it is not a medical diagnosis and there is no proven association with implants, though some patients report improvement after removal.Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021) MammographyImplants interfere with mammography because X-rays cannot pass through them; tell the screening service you have implants so special views can be taken, and the more breast volume that is implant the greater the problem; some patients choose private MRI screening.Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021) Breastfeeding and pregnancyImplants do not interfere with the ability to breastfeed, though some evidence suggests milk production may be reduced; pregnancy and breastfeeding may adversely affect the shape of the breast.Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021) MythsIt is safe to sunbathe and fly with implants; implant massage is not needed and is not recommended with modern textured implants.Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021) Fat transfer alternativeLipofilling is the only alternative surgical technique to enlarge the breast; only a relatively small amount of fat can be injected so multiple operations are needed, some fat is absorbed early, and fat that lasts brings permanent enlargement — your own fat is the only substance that can be safely injected.Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021) UpliftMastopexy lifts the nipple and breast tissue and tightens skin without an implant; where both volume loss and droopiness are concerns, augmentation with mastopexy — as one operation or two stages — should be discussed.Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021) Implant registryThe UK Breast and Cosmetic Implant Registry records all implants placed or removed so patients can be traced in a future recall; entry requires consent and is strongly recommended for anyone having implant-based surgery.Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021) Implant safety approvalBreast implants continue to have safety approval from government organisations such as the UK MHRA and USA FDA and continue to be used in breast reconstruction worldwide.Breast Implant Safety BIA-SCC and other lymphomasIn July 2023 BAAPS issued a joint statement on Breast Implant Associated Squamous Cell Carcinoma and other breast implant associated lymphomas.Breast Implant Safety PIP implantsThe 2013 expert group found no evidence PIP implants increased breast cancer rate, but the gel was less cohesive and had greater potential to cause local inflammation; BAAPS advised removal or replacement as a precaution.Breast Implant Safety PIP warning signsSigns of PIP rupture, leak or inflammation include breast lumpiness, lymph node swelling, change in shape or size, redness, tenderness, swelling and firmness; symptoms may include pain and hypersensitivity.Breast Implant Safety Consumer decisionOnly you can decide whether to go ahead with aesthetic surgery; no procedure is 100% risk free and no surgeon can give a 100% guarantee of results.BAAPS Consumer Safety Guidelines Cooling-off (consumer guidance)You should expect a two-week cooling-off period following your consultation, and should avoid booking fees, non-refundable advances and any technique that traps you into proceeding.BAAPS Consumer Safety Guidelines Surgeon credentialsYour consultation should be with the surgeon who will operate, and a specialist plastic surgeon should have FCRS (Plast) and be on the GMC Specialist Register of Plastic Surgeons.BAAPS Consumer Safety Guidelines Timing and supportAvoid surgery around major life events, consider travel and insurance implications carefully, talk to your GP, and take as much time as you need — you can cancel up until the time you go to sleep for surgery.BAAPS Consumer Safety Guidelines Statements are paraphrased from BAAPS patient information and the joint ABS, BAAPS and BAPRAS booklet (Edition 2, 2021). (3)Continuing Education ActivityStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18The review's opening summary: breast augmentation increases breast size, most often with an implant and less commonly with fat transfer, and is among the most commonly performed plastic surgery procedures in the United States. It frames the activity around indications, contraindications, complications and the role of the interprofessional team before and after surgery.Objectives are to identify the different techniques, describe the indications, review the complications and improve care coordination among the team.The FDA restricted silicone-filled implants for cosmetic enhancement from 1992; reconstructive patients continued to receive them after mastectomy.The activity is written for the interprofessional team involved in pre- and postoperative care.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →IntroductionStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Breast augmentation is a surgical procedure in which breast size is enhanced, either by placing an implant or, less commonly, through fat transfer. The section traces FDA policy on silicone implants from the 1992 restriction to the 2006 reversal, describes the shift towards cohesive gel and form-stable implants, and sets out monitoring advice and the fact that implants are not permanent devices.Extensive research failed to confirm the disease fears that led to the 1992 silicone restriction, and the FDA allowed general use of silicone-filled implants again in 2006.By 2017 the majority of patients undergoing augmentation received cohesive gel silicone implants, with makers introducing different levels of gel firmness.The FDA recommends MRI screening every two years in patients with silicone implants to detect subclinical leaks, but adherence is incomplete and MRI readings can be false positive.Higher gel cohesion may lower rupture rates, but the review states that eventually all implants will rupture or break.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →Anatomy and PhysiologyStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18The anatomy relevant to augmentation: the breast sits on the anterior chest wall below the clavicle, bounded medially by the sternum, laterally by the latissimus dorsi and inferiorly by the inframammary fold, with the pectoralis muscles forming its posterior boundary.The inframammary fold is a dermal structure formed by fusion of the superficial and mammary fascia.Blood supply comes from the subdermal plexus with major contributions from the internal mammary artery, external mammary artery and intercostal perforators.Nerve supply is mainly through the intercostal plexus, with most contribution from the third to fifth intercostal nerves.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →Indications and contraindicationsWho the review says the procedure is for, and the conditions that should stop a surgeon from operating. (2)IndicationsStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Implants are placed for reconstruction after mastectomy, for developmental disorders such as hypomastia, and for elective reasons related to self-image. Hypomastia may follow normal development or involution, especially after pregnancy, and people of all personality types may seek the procedure.Reported motivations include reconstruction, developmental under-development of the breast and elective enhancement of self-image.The review notes that when surveyed after surgery, the vast majority of women would undergo the operation again.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →ContraindicationsStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Most patients have no contraindications, but the review lists the conditions that should prevent surgery and the patient factors that should pause it.Absolute reasons not to operate include active infection of the breast, active cancer and pregnancy.Relative reasons include a history of autoimmune disease, current radiation treatment, unstable medical conditions and known sensitivity to silicone.Psychological instability or unrealistic expectations are also given as reasons not to proceed.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →The operationEquipment, theatre team, preparation, implant choices, placement, incisions, anaesthesia, duration and expected recovery. (4)EquipmentStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Routine operating-room equipment is usually sufficient. Extras depend on the approach: a lighted retractor or headlight for visualising the pocket, an endoscope for umbilical or axillary approaches, and sometimes an implant sleeve used as part of a no-touch technique.A no-touch technique limits handling of the implant to reduce implant trauma and bacterial contamination.Endoscopic equipment may be required when the umbilical or axillary route is used.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →PersonnelStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18The operating team normally consists of the surgeon, a scrubbed assistant, an anaesthesiologist and a circulating nurse working together in the operating room.Standard theatre roles apply: surgeon, scrubbed assistant, anaesthesiologist and circulating nurse.The team structure is described as the same as for other routine surgical procedures.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →PreparationStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Patients are prepared for surgery as for any other surgical procedure, following the usual preoperative pathway.Preparation follows the routine preoperative work-up used for any operation, including assessment and consent.The review places emphasis on informed consent and on the pre-operative teaching that reduces later problems.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →Technique or TreatmentStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Two main implant types are described, saline-filled and silicone-filled, both with a silicone outer shell that can be smooth or textured. Implants can sit above or beneath the pectoralis muscle, be reached through inframammary, transaxillary or peri-areolar incisions, and are usually done as an outpatient operation under general anaesthesia.Saline implants are inserted empty and filled through a port, typically with a 25 to 50 mL range specified by the manufacturer.Saline implants are FDA-approved from age 18 for augmentation and at any age for reconstruction; silicone gel implants are approved from age 22.Silicone implants suit patients with thin soft-tissue coverage better, showing less rippling and a softer, more natural feel.Texturing prevents rotation in shaped implants and may lower capsular contracture in the subglandular pocket, but not in the submuscular pocket.No single placement method is uniformly accepted as best; the choice is made jointly by patient and surgeon.The operation generally takes 45 to 90 minutes; most patients return to light work within a week, with full activity taking up to six weeks.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →Complications and outcomesEarly and late complications, capsular contracture, implant longevity, reported satisfaction and how the care team reduces risk. (4)ComplicationsStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Complication rates are described as low, but no implant is a lifetime device. Early problems include infection, bleeding and sensory change; later problems include malposition, deflation or leak and capsular contracture, which may require further surgery.Surgeons commonly estimate a 15 to 20 year lifespan for implants, with no uniform recommendation on routine replacement.Early complications listed are infection, scarring, asymmetry, haematoma, seroma, breast pain, poor cosmetic outcome and changes in nipple or breast sensation.Later complications listed are implant malposition or displacement, implant deflation or leak, and capsular contracture.Capsular contracture is graded 1 to 4 and may require surgical correction or implant removal when severe.Staphylococcus epidermidis and Cutibacterium acnes are the microorganisms most commonly isolated in studies of capsular contracture, supporting a suspected biofilm or low-grade infection mechanism.A slim possibility of breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) is reported, possibly linked to a particular type of implant texturing, although the exact relationship is not yet determined.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →Clinical SignificanceStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18The procedure remains highly popular, and the review stresses that clinicians treating women with implants should be aware of them, because the implants are relevant to other conditions and to screening.The American Society of Plastic Surgeons reported approximately 290,000 augmentation procedures performed in the United States in 2016.The vast majority of patients report improved self-esteem and satisfaction with the decision.Doctors treating these patients for other conditions should have an awareness of the procedure and of implants in general.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →Enhancing Healthcare Team OutcomesStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Risk reduction is described as a team effort: informed consent, nurse-led preoperative instruction, smoking cessation, pharmacist medicines checks and early recognition of problems. Outcomes are reported as good, with most patients pleased with the result.Many past litigations arose primarily from a lack of informed consent, which the pre-operative visit is meant to address.Patients should be instructed to stop smoking and make positive lifestyle changes so results last longer.Pharmacists contribute by checking allergies and explaining medicines, which can reduce infection and help pain control.Surveys cited in the review indicate about 70 to 80 percent of patients are satisfied and feel the outcome was perfect.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →References and Further ReadingStatPearls reference list · Last updated 2023-07-18The review cites twelve sources spanning secondary augmentation, transgender breast contouring, anatomical versus round implants, fat grafting, capsular contracture risk factors, cosmetic-tourism infection, subclinical implant infection, outcomes series and long-term follow-up.The full reference list, with links to each PubMed record, is reproduced in the references section of this page.Every citation can be checked at source through its PMID link.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov → Extracted data Key facts from the review The statements below summarise what the StatPearls review says about breast augmentation. The article covers the two implant fills (sterile saline and silicone), the outpatient or hospital setting, general versus local anaesthetic, the four usual incision routes, how implant and technique choices affect pain, appearance, implant integrity and future mammograms, the reasons for surgery, the risks (including capsular contracture, implant rupture, breast implant-associated lymphoma and reported systemic symptoms), what to arrange before the operation, what happens afterwards, and the expected outcome.Augmentation is done by placing an implant behind the breast tissue or beneath the chest muscle, and implants are sacs filled with either sterile salt water or silicone.The operation is performed at an outpatient surgery clinic or in a hospital, most often under general anaesthetic, with local anaesthetic as an alternative.Four incision routes are described: the natural fold under the breast (the most common), the armpit using an endoscope, the edge of the areola, and, for saline implants only, a route near the navel through which the empty implant is tunnelled and then filled.An areola-edge incision may bring more difficulty with breastfeeding and more loss of nipple sensation, and may carry a higher risk of capsular contracture.Implant type, implant size and the chosen operation influence post-operative pain, the appearance achieved, the chance of later breakage or leakage, and the extra views future mammograms will need.Reasons for the procedure include increasing breast size, changing breast shape and correcting a congenital deformity; patients are told to expect improvement rather than perfection.Risks shared with any operation are listed as reactions to medicines, breathing problems, bleeding, blood clots and infection.Breast-specific risks include difficulty breastfeeding, numbness around the nipple or surrounding skin, small or thickened raised scars, uneven nipple position, differences in size or shape between the two breasts, implant breakage or leakage, visible rippling, infection requiring implant removal, the need for more breast surgery and puncture of the lung.A capsule of scar tissue normally forms around a new implant; when it thickens it can change the breast's shape, harden the breast tissue or cause pain.A rare immune-system cancer, breast implant-associated lymphoma, has been reported with some implants, presenting as a mass or swelling around the implant with breast pain and treated by removing the implant and the tissue around it.Some people report systemic symptoms after implants — grouped under breast implant illness, which the page says is not yet established as a recognised illness — including fatigue, memory and concentration problems, joint and muscle pain, anxiety, hair loss, depression, rash, autoimmune disease, inflammation and weight change; some improve after removal and some do not.Before surgery patients should ask about a screening mammogram, disclose any pregnancy possibility and every medicine or supplement they take, review diabetes, heart disease and other conditions, stop smoking (which slows healing and raises clot risk), prepare the home and arrange transport and help for one to two days.During the week before surgery, blood thinners such as aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen and vitamin E are commonly paused on the surgeon's advice, and fasting and morning-medicine instructions come from the surgical team.Afterwards the breasts are wrapped in bulky gauze or a surgical bra, drainage tubes are removed within about three days, and massaging from around day five may be suggested to reduce capsular hardening after checking with the provider.Outcomes are usually very good, scars are permanent and most visible during the first year before fading, a supportive bra may be worn for a few months, and later tests may be advised to confirm the implants are intact.Read the original on medlineplus.gov →Recovery, discharge and wound carePatient instructions for the days and weeks after cosmetic breast surgery, plus general guidance for looking after a surgical incision that has been left open.Cosmetic breast surgery - dischargePatient instructions · Page last reviewed 2025-02-17Home-care instructions after cosmetic breast surgery — augmentation, lift or reduction. Definition and context Breast enlargement as natural mammoplasia or active intervention, and why breasts matter to self-image, femininity and sexual attractiveness. Surgical method Breast augmentation with implants or fat transfer, listed as an actual and potential method and linked to the augmentation articles. Hormonal method Pharmacological or hormonal enhancement with medications such as estrogen or breast enlargement supplements, with three supporting citations. Food energy and KLF14 Increasing food energy intake to add adipose tissue near the breast area, with distribution between individuals controlled by the KLF14 gene. Mechanical method Mechanical breast enhancement, cited to a 2007 study of the Brava external tissue expander. Ineffective methods The Mark Eden bust developer, named and described as a fraudulently marketed method and device. The article in briefBreast enlargement is the enlargement of the breasts. It may occur naturally as in mammoplasia or may occur artificially through active intervention. Many women regard their breasts, which are female secondary sex characteristics, as important to their sexual attractiveness, as a sign of femininity that is important to their sense of self. Due to this, when a woman considers her breasts deficient in some respect, she might choose to engage in some activity intended to enhance them.Mammoplasia. The article names natural breast enlargement as mammoplasia, distinguishing it from enlargement produced by active intervention. reconstruction, trauma and explantation deformity; micromastia, tuberous breast deformity and Poland syndrome; and primary aesthetic augmentation.Developed by Melvin Bircoll; in 1987 Eduardo Krulig injected grafts with a syringe and blunt needle using a disposable fat trap.Up to about 300 ml of body fat can be injected in three equal-volume injections across subpectoral, intrapectoral and submammary spaces.Risks: fat necrosis, metastatic calcification, cysts and palpable lumps.Adding adipose-derived stem cells raised graft success rates in a 2007 40-patient study.Read this section on Wikipedia →Fat grafting techniquesArticle sectionHarvesting, centrifugal refinement, blunt-cannula injection in small aliquots, and how much of the graft survives.Only about 25–50% of transferred fat survives at one year, so compensatory over-filling is used.Small-aliquot blunt-cannula injection maximises contact with vascularised tissue and minimises fat necrosis.Contours are sculpted by layering grafts at different depths — from the chest wall to just under the skin.Operating time: about 2 hours for the first 100 cm³, then about 45 minutes per extra 100 cm³.Fat grafted around an implant can hide device edges and wrinkles and soften the capsule.Read this section on Wikipedia →External tissue expansionArticle sectionVacuum pre-expansion of the recipient site before fat grafting, with the reported volume gains from two studies.In a 17-woman study, a bra-like vacuum system applied 20 mmHg for 10–12 hours daily over 10 weeks.Average volume gain at week 10 was about 98%, with a stable long-term increase of 55% (range 15–115%).A 2010 study of 25 patients (46 breasts) reported significant volume increases of 60–200% at six months by MRI, with no oil cysts or abnormality.MRI and 3-D volumetric imaging are used to monitor graft viability and volume maintenance.Read this section on Wikipedia →Post-mastectomy proceduresArticle sectionImplant and flap reconstruction options, and fat-graft reconstruction as a non-implant alternative.Surgical options include implants, TRAM flap, latissimus myocutaneous flap and DIEP flap.Fat-graft reconstruction begins with 3–5 weeks of external vacuum expansion, then serial grafting sessions over about three months.Some reconstructions begin in the operating room at the mastectomy itself, seeding fat into the recipient site.Reported outcomes: natural form and near-normal sensation, with resumption of normal activities at about 3 days.Read this section on Wikipedia →Tissue engineering: the breast mound and explantation deformityArticle sectionPre-expanded, fat-seeded breast mounds after mastectomy, and using fat grafts to correct empty implant pockets after explantation.A 2010 series: 33 women (47 breasts) pre-expanded for 10 hours daily over 10–30 days, then grafted with 150–600 ml per session across 2–5 outpatient procedures.Stable reconstructed volumes of 300–600 ml per breast at six months, with benign oil cysts and rare complications (pneumothorax, transient cysts).After implant removal, fat grafts replace about 50% of the removed volume as permanent augmentation.Fat cannot survive in an empty implant pocket — it must be injected into a vascularised tissue matrix.Read this section on Wikipedia →Fat-graft augmentation outcomes and limitationsArticle sectionReported volume gains from fat grafting and why it cannot replace the volumes implants deliver.A 2010 study of 25 patients: mean breast volume increased 1.2× (60–80%, about 250 cm³ per breast) at six months, confirmed by quantitative MRI.Graft volumes of 220–650 cm³ per breast; mean operating time 2 hours; no infection, cyst, seroma, haematoma or necrosis reported.Structural fat grafting gives precise contour control but cannot achieve the large global volume increases implants provide.In one session, even patients with ample donor fat gained about one bra cup size.Radiotherapy of an implant-augmented breast sharply raises complication rates (contracture, infection, extrusion, poor cosmetic outcome).Read this section on Wikipedia →Function and safetyBreastfeeding with implants, breast-filler toxicity and platinum toxicity.Breastfeeding and the prosthetic breastArticle sectionWhether implants interfere with breastfeeding, and which surgical choices preserve lactation.Women with implants can breastfeed, but surgery that cuts into the nipple-areola complex can damage ducts or nerves.IMF, transaxillary and transumbilical approaches avoid the nipple-areola complex.Subglandular placement and oversized implants interfere most with lactation; small implants in a submuscular pocket interfere least.Filler leakage into milk is considered a minimal risk: silicone is indigestible and saline digestible.A 1996 study found no causal link between prostheses and impaired breastfeeding function.Read this section on Wikipedia →Breast-filler toxicity and platinum toxicityArticle sectionTheoretical filler transfer to milk, and the platinum catalyst used to make silicone gel — both reviewed as minimal risks.Breast-filler toxicity is described as a minimal risk to a nursing infant because silicone is indigestible and saline digestible.Platinum (Pt 78) is the catalyst that turns liquid silicone oil into gel; trace platinum could theoretically accumulate in bone marrow.The FDA found the platinum in modern implants is not ionised and poses no biological risk, with no reported cases of trace-platinum toxicity.Read this section on Wikipedia →The patientPsychology before surgery, outcomes reported afterwards, women bodybuilders and mental-health findings.Psychology of breast-augmentation patientsArticle sectionMental-health characteristics of women seeking augmentation, and the outcomes they report after surgery.Pre-operative studies report more prior psychotherapy, low self-esteem, depression and body dysmorphia than in the general population.Post-operative surveys report improved physical health, appearance, social life, confidence, self-esteem and sexual functioning.Most women report long-term satisfaction with their implants, even after revision surgery.About 8% of Danish augmentation patients had a pre-operative psychiatric hospitalization history.Read this section on Wikipedia →Mental health and mortality findingsArticle sectionSuicide and mortality findings, and measured self-esteem gains — with the article's conclusion on causation.A 2007 longitudinal study found higher suicide rates among women with implants over time, alongside higher alcohol- and drug-related death risk.The article's conclusion: surgery does not increase suicide risk — it is the psychologically affected woman who is more likely to seek augmentation.A 2007 study reported self-esteem gains of 20.7–24.9 points on the 30-point Rosenberg scale after surgery.Plastic surgeons are advised to assess mental health before operating, to judge whether implants can genuinely help.Read this section on Wikipedia → Surgical technique Five types of surgical incision How the prosthesis reaches the implant pocket — and what each route means for scars, access and breastfeeding. Five types of surgical incision IncisionWhat the article says Inframammary incisionA cut at the inframammary fold (the bottom border of the breast) giving maximal access to the interior of the breast for precise pocket creation and implant placement. Scarring can be noticeable depending on skin type. Periareolar incisionA short (~5 cm) cut along the lower half of the areola's outer border. The narrow access makes large silicone implants harder to place, tends toward higher capsular contracture rates long term, and risks damaging milk ducts and nerves of the nipple-areola complex, which can impede breastfeeding. It also permits a concurrent breast lift. Transaxillary incisionA cut in the armpit with a tunnel under the skin to the breast pocket, done bluntly or with an endoscope. It avoids scarring the breast skin; the challenge is judging the ideal implant position for symmetry. Transumbilical incision (TUBA)An endoscopic approach through the navel, tunneling upward under the abdominal skin to place a saline implant. It avoids scarring the breast skin. Transabdominal incision (TABA)An endoscopic approach through the navel tunneling up to the breast pocket, performed while the patient simultaneously undergoes an abdominoplasty. Condensed from the “Types of surgical incision” section. The incision route is chosen with the surgeon according to anatomy, implant type and goals. Surgical technique Four implant-pocket placements Placements described in anatomical relation to the pectoralis major muscle. Four implant-pocket placements PlacementWhat the article says SubglandularThe implant sits between the breast tissue and the pectoralis major muscle (retromammary space), closest to the natural breast plane and usually the most aesthetic — but more prone to visible rippling in women with little soft tissue. SubfascialThe implant is placed beneath the fascia covering the pectoralis major muscle, to add size and volume for later contouring. Subpectoral (dual plane)The implant is placed beneath the pectoralis major muscle after partially releasing its lower attachments: the upper half of the implant is covered by muscle, the lower half sits in the subglandular plane. It maximizes upper coverage and lower expansion, at some risk of animation deformity (the implant moving with the muscle). SubmuscularThe implant is placed entirely beneath the pectoralis major muscle without cutting its lower origin; total coverage can be completed by releasing and reattaching lateral chest-wall muscles (serratus or pectoralis minor). Condensed from the “Implant-pocket placement” section. Placement affects coverage, rippling risk, recovery and how the implant moves. Implant types The four prosthesis types The four categories of breast prosthesis the article describes, two of which are discontinued. The four prosthesis types ProsthesisCategorySummaryDetail Saline breast prosthesisImplant typeA silicone-elastic shell filled with sterile saline solution in the operating room.First sold commercially by Laboratoires Arion of France in 1964. The empty shell is inserted through a short incision, then filled with saline and contoured for symmetry. Results are good to excellent, but rippling and wrinkling of the skin can show, especially in women with little breast tissue; with ample tissue and submuscular placement, results resemble those of silicone-gel implants. Silicone-gel breast prosthesisImplant typeA shell filled with viscous silicone gel; the technology has passed through five generations of design.Invented in 1961 by Frank Gerow and Thomas Cronin, made by Dow Corning, and first used in augmentation in 1962. Generation 1 (1963) was a teardrop silicone-rubber sack with a Dacron fastener patch. Generation 2 (1970s) used thin shells and low-cohesion gel — fragile, with higher rupture, leakage and capsular contracture rates that prompted class-action lawsuits; polyurethane-coated variants reduced contracture but were dropped in the U.S. over carcinogenic TDA by-products (they remain in use in Europe and South America); double-lumen designs combined gel and saline with post-operative volume adjustability. Generations 3 and 4 (1980s) added elastomer coatings to reduce gel bleed, with shaped, tapered and round textured or smooth models. Generation 5 (1990s) uses semi-solid cohesive gel that resists leakage and migration, with studies reporting lower capsular contracture and rupture rates than earlier generations. Alternative-composition breast prosthesisImplant type (discontinued)Fillers such as soy oil, polypropylene string, ox cartilage, Terylene wool, ground rubber, silastic or Teflon-silicone — now discontinued.The article lists these fillers as substances harmful to the body and no longer in use. Structured breast prosthesisImplant type (discontinued)Nested silicone-rubber shells with saline between them, approved by the FDA and Health Canada in 2014; now discontinued.Three nested shells support the upper half of the breast and the two spaces between them are filled with saline, combining saline and silicone technologies. The folded empty device is inserted, then filled with saline and the incision sutured. Condensed from the “Breast-augmentation prostheses” section. Implant availability differs by country and regulator. Extracted data Key facts from the article The statements below condense what the Wikipedia article says about breast augmentation. The right-hand column links to the source article. Key facts from the article TopicWhat the article saysSource DefinitionBreast augmentation (also breast enlargement) is a plastic surgery procedure placing a breast implant or fat graft on the thorax to increase breast size, correct congenital defects and restore anatomic proportion.Breast augmentation Three purposesProsthetic breasts are placed for three therapeutic reasons: primary reconstruction after cancer, trauma or developmental defect; revision of a previous mammoplasty; and primary aesthetic augmentation.Breast augmentation Fat-graft gainA fat-graft augmentation yields a modest size increase — usually about one bra cup size — because the body resorbs much of the injected fat.Breast augmentation Saline historyThe first commercial saline-filled breast prosthesis was presented by Laboratoires Arion of France in 1964.Breast augmentation Silicone historyThe silicone-gel implant was invented in 1961 by Frank Gerow and Thomas Cronin, made by Dow Corning, and first used for augmentation in 1962; its technology spans five generations.Breast augmentation Structured implantsStructured (nested-shell) breast prostheses were approved by the FDA and Health Canada in 2014; both structured and alternative-composition prostheses are now discontinued.Breast augmentation IncisionsFive surgical incision routes are used: inframammary, periareolar, transaxillary, transumbilical (TUBA) and transabdominal (TABA).Breast augmentation PlacementsFour implant-pocket placements are described: subglandular, subfascial, subpectoral (dual plane) and submuscular.Breast augmentation RecoveryScars heal at about 6 weeks, most patients resume normal activities at about 1 week, and strenuous exercise is avoided for about 6 weeks; submuscular placement means a longer, more painful recovery.Breast augmentation Complication rateComplications from implant surgery and tissue expanders occur in approximately 6–7% of breast-augmentation patients.Breast augmentation Explantation at 10 yearsAbout 20% of women with aesthetic implants and 50% of reconstruction patients required explantation of a failed prosthesis at the 10-year mark.Breast augmentation BIA-ALCL recallIn 2019 the FDA recalled all Allergan Biocell textured breast prostheses after a causal link was identified with BIA-ALCL, an immune-system cancer.Breast augmentation Rupture detectionManual examination detects only about 30% of implant ruptures, while MRI detects about 86%; the FDA recommends screening MRI at 3 years post-surgery and every 2 years thereafter for suspected rupture.Breast augmentation Saline rupture ratesReported saline rupture-and-deflation rates are 3–5% at 3 years and 7–10% at 10 years; overfilling implants by about 10–13% reduced the 8-year deflation rate to 1.83%.Breast augmentation Revision ratesRevision (re-operation) rates were reported as 20% at 3 years and 3.0% at 7 years in the article's cited Tebbetts data.Breast augmentation Systemic diseaseReviews and longitudinal studies since the 1990s consistently report no causal relation between silicone-gel implants and systemic or autoimmune disease.Breast augmentation Fat survivalOnly about 25–50% of a fat graft survives at one year, so grafts are deliberately over-filled; retained contours typically last 18–24 months.Breast augmentation Fat-graft volume gainA 2010 clinical-radiological study reported a mean breast-volume increase of 1.2× (60–80%, about 250 cm³ per breast) at 6 months after fat grafting, confirmed by quantitative MRI.Breast augmentation External expansionExternal vacuum pre-expansion (20 mmHg, 10–12 hours daily for 10 weeks) produced an average 98% volume gain at week 10, settling to a stable 55% long-term increase (range 15–115%).Breast augmentation BreastfeedingSmall implants in a submuscular pocket interfere least with breastfeeding; subglandular placement and oversized implants interfere most, and IMF/TABA/TUBA approaches avoid the nipple-areola complex.Breast augmentation Self-esteemA 2007 study reported post-operative self-esteem increases of 20.7–24.9 points on the 30-point Rosenberg scale, alongside reports of improved confidence and sexual functioning.Breast augmentation Mental-health cautionThe article notes higher pre-operative rates of depression, low self-esteem and body dysmorphia among augmentation seekers, and concludes that underlying psychological factors — not the surgery itself — explain the suicide-risk correlation reported in longitudinal studies.Breast augmentation RadiotherapyRadiotherapy of an implant-augmented breast much increases complication rates — capsular contracture, infection, extrusion and poor cosmetic outcome — which can preclude conservative breast surgery.Breast augmentation Statements are paraphrased from the Wikipedia article.
